query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor boron addition (~0.1 at%) into an AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA), followed by homogenization and rolling, will refine the lamellar microstructure and strengthen grain boundaries, thereby simultaneously increasing both the yield strength and ductility relative to the same EHEA without boron.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy prepared by vacuum arc melting.
generation.intervention: Add ~0.1 at% B to the base EHEA composition and perform standard homogenization (e.g., ~1100 °C, 24 h) followed by rolling.
generation.conditions: Eutectic AlCoCrFeNi alloy with boron addition, homogenized in vacuum or inert atmosphere at ~1100 °C, then rolled to significant reduction (e.g., 50–70%).
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregates to and strengthens grain/lamellar boundaries, refining the lamellar spacing and inhibiting crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: Minor B addition improves boundary cohesion and refines the lamellae, which enhances dislocation trapping and impedes crack growth, leading to a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline EHEA without boron, the B-doped alloy is expected to exhibit moderately higher yield strength (on the order of 5–15%) and a measurable improvement in elongation to failure (on the order of a few percentage points).
generation.baseline: Identical AlCoCrFeNi-based EHEA composition and processing without boron addition.
generation.boundary: Boron should remain at low levels (~0.1 at%) to avoid brittle phases. The improvement may depend on rolling reduction and annealing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitudes depend on specific processing conditions and potential boride formation; further experiments are needed to confirm any optimal doping level.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two EHEAs, one with ~0.1 at% B and one without, via vacuum arc melting. Homogenize both at ~1100 °C for 24 h, then roll to a comparable reduction. Compare their microstructures (SEM/TEM) and tensile properties at room temperature.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and phase distribution via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the B-doped alloy does not exhibit both higher yield strength (≥5% increase) and similar or improved ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural refinement and grain boundary strengthening by B are not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. Because the designs of equiatomic HEAs still impose various restrictions in terms of alloy composition and properties, the concept of nonequiatomic HEAs have been proposed [,]. This innovative design not only retains the characteristics of HEAs but also substantially expands the scope of HEA designs []. Subsequently, nonequiatomic HEAs with multiphase structures and MEAs were proposed; these alloys exhibit favorable properties and retain the effects of HEAs, and they represent a new chapter in the design and development of future alloys [,,]. In addition, nonequiatomic alloys are more flexible than equiatomic HEAs in terms of alloy composition adjustments, which are performed to prevent the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds [,]. Moreover, some studies showed that the MEAs present outstanding mechanical properties, which indicates that the MEAs possess a huge potential in the applications of industry [,,]. In addition to alloy composition adjustments, the mechanical properties of nonequiatomic alloys can also be further improved through processes such as rolling or forging [,,]. Microstructural modifications of HEAs based on mechanical processing, thermomechanical processing and elemental additions have been explored in order to obtain better combinations of mechanical properties. Severe plastic deformation of the CoCrFeMnNi FCC HEA through high pressure torsion was found to result in a large increase in both hardness (520 HV) and strength (1950 MPa), but the development of nano-crystalline microstructure (~ 50 nm) made the alloy brittle. Introduction of twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) to the CoCrFeMnNi HEA was found to impart good strain-hardening ability, resulting in a large tensile ductility, albeit at the cost of low values of true ultimate tensile strength (1124 MPa). The use of shot peening to develop a hierarchical microstructure (consisting of a thin deformed layer and an un-deformed core) in a CoCrFeMnNi HEA resulted in a strength increase, but the improvement was limited to only around 700 MPa. chosen.why: Microalloying with boron is a straightforward single-step modification widely used to enhance grain boundary cohesion and refine microstructure. In eutectic high-entropy alloys for structural applications, small additions of B can promote a fine lamellar microstructure and stabilize grain boundaries, improving both strength and ductility. This is consistent with prior studies in related materials, and it offers a direct, well-known pathway to address the question of achieving simultaneous strengthening and toughening.
